media:group.media:title: Learning How to Listen
media:group.media:description:
This conversation explores a central topic: How can oral historians listen closely, critically, and imaginatively to silences and emotion? How might speculative and creative practices preserve dimensions of testimony that exceed both language and transcription? What, finally, are the ethical challenges of documenting endangered oral traditions or stories of violence?
Over many years, the panelists have worked closely with Canadian World War veterans; women who participated in the Lebanese Civil War; Chinese-speaking immigrant women who experienced intimate partner violence; and the Mirasi community of Punjab. For all four panelists, relationality lies at the core of their commitment to non-extractivist research. Their research affords an extended contemplation of the principle of “Sharing Authority,” so foundational to our work at COHDS. In essence, panelists are reflecting on what we are doing to try and “make oral history a more democratic cultural practice.” (Zembrzycki, 2009)

entry.title: Le récit du corps traumatisé avec Marie-Josée Gicali

media:group.media:title: Le récit du corps traumatisé avec Marie-Josée Gicali
media:group.media:description:
Ce projet est né de l’histoire personnelle de Marie-Josée en tant que rescapée du génocide contre les Tutsi au Rwanda. Une cicatrice sur son bras, souvenir d'une violence extrême, est devenue le point de départ d'une réflexion plus vaste sur les traces que le génocide a laissées sur les corps et les âmes des survivants. Blessée par balle lors des massacres de 1994, elle a longtemps porté cette cicatrice comme un stigmate. Aujourd'hui, elle est devenue un témoin, un support de mémoire et un point d'ancrage pour une démarche de recherche, de création et de transmission.
À partir de cette expérience, Marie-Josée a entrepris de rencontrer d'autres rescapé.e.s qui portent, eux aussi, des cicatrices et des mutilations causées par le génocide contre les Tutsi. Son intention n'est pas de raviver la souffrance, mais de rendre visibles les conséquences durables de cette violence extrême, tout en mettant en lumière la dignité, le courage et la résilience de celles et ceux qui ont survécu. Le corps devient ainsi un lieu de mémoire, de témoignage et de résistance.
Trente ans après le génocide, les séquelles physiques et psychologiques demeurent profondément inscrites dans les corps, les esprits et la mémoire collective. Si les archives historiques ont largement documenté les événements de 1994, les cicatrices visibles et invisibles des survivants continuent de raconter une histoire qui reste à transmettre. La photographie et le documentaire constituent des moyens privilégiés pour préserver ces récits, susciter le dialogue et contribuer à une mémoire vivante.
Ce panel proposera une réflexion sur les enjeux méthodologiques, éthiques et humains de cette recherche photographique et documentaire. Il abordera notamment les défis liés à la collecte de témoignages sur un sujet aussi sensible, ainsi que la posture de la chercheure, à la fois survivante, témoin et productrice de savoirs. Cette double position soulève des questions importantes quant à la proximité avec les participants, à l'empathie, aux avantages et aux limites d'une recherche menée de l’intérieur et de l'extérieur.
Les discussions porteront également sur le consentement éclairé, la dignité des personnes photographiées et interviewées, la sensibilité aux traumatismes, la prévention de la revictimisation et les modalités d'accompagnement des témoins. Ce panel mettra en évidence la responsabilité des chercheurs, des photographes et des documentaristes dans la construction d'une mémoire fidèle aux expériences vécues et respectueuse des personnes. Il montrera enfin comment la recherche visuelle et documentaire peut contribuer à la transmission de la mémoire, à la lutte contre le négationnisme et à la promotion des droits humains.

entry.title: Memories of Migration with Andrew Jackson

media:group.media:title: Memories of Migration with Andrew Jackson
media:group.media:description:
Join us for a screening of three moving-image works, accompanied by an artist talk discussing these films alongside existing and forthcoming projects from Andrew Jackson's wider photographic and interdisciplinary practice. The programme comprises The Weight of Light (27 minutes), In Heart and Life and Longing, Part 2: Family Over Fame (20 minutes), and In Heart and Life and Longing, Part 3: Full Circle (19 minutes).
Across photography and moving image, Jackson's work considers family, migration, Black diasporic experience, memory and the political histories embedded within landscapes and everyday life. These films emerge from a sustained interest in the relationship between Jamaica, Britain and Canada, and in the ways that identity is formed through movement, aspiration, intimacy, loss and inheritance.
Moving between Quebec, Ghana, Jamaica and the United Kingdom, The Weight of Light considers migration, racialisation and the traces of colonial violence that landscapes can reveal, conceal and carry. It asks how land becomes a repository for histories that may no longer be immediately visible, but which continue to shape how places are understood, inhabited and remembered. The two films in the In Heart and Life and Longing series focus more closely on family, masculinity and the emotional weight of migration. Rather than treating their subjects as illustrations of wider social questions, the films make room for speech, silence, humour and contradiction. They resist simple narratives of success, failure or belonging.
The accompanying artist talk would place the films in dialogue with Jackson's wider practice, including Little Burgundy, The Sentence Stays With Me, a Canada Council for the Arts-funded post-documentary project on the enduring effects of incarceration after release; The Ground Beneath Us: Black Cartographies of Montreal, which examines Black spatial experience across Montréal. Together, the screening and talk would offer audiences an opportunity to engage with the moving-image works in depth, while also considering the research, ethical questions and lived encounters that shape my approach to photography and film.

media:group.media:title: Memories of the Border
media:group.media:description:
Join us for readings and screenings of selections from "Memories of the Border" followed by a discussion with those involved in the making of the series.
Since the summer of 2025, Montreal-based Solidarity Across Borders (SAB), a migrant justice network comprised of migrants and supporters, has been in collaboration with Concordia’s Feminist Media Studio (FMS) to create a community-led oral history project called “Memories of the Border”. Together, FMS and SAB work to create an interview testimonial series, giving voice to the experiences of undocumented migrants, tracing their journeys, their difficulties, and their hopes, while humanizing a reality that is too often invisible.
This project hopes to create an awareness-raising and advocacy tool for the regularization of undocumented migrants, provide a collective memory that bears witness to their presence and contribution to society, all while strengthening community solidarity by highlighting the voices of those whose experiences are often reduced to political debates and public discourse, rather than recognized through the complexity of their everyday lives.
Through this conversation, we hope to receive feedback on our work-in-progress and have a fruitful discussion about the power of community storytelling in contributing to political and social action, along with what it means, personally, to find empowerment in having one’s own story be heard, witnessed, and felt.

entry.title: Décoloniser les salons du livre d’art et l’éducation en design

media:group.media:title: Décoloniser les salons du livre d’art et l’éducation en design
media:group.media:description:
avec Pascale Obolo et Marly Jean-Noel & Victoria Owusu
Alors que le réseau international des salons du livre d’art ne cesse de s’étendre, quelles mesures organisationnelles et ambitieuses les salons peuvent-ils mettre en œuvre pour garantir la représentation des pays du Sud? Une discussion animée par Pascale Obolo, coauteure du guide pratique « Decolonizing Art Book Fairs » et fondatrice de l’African Art Book Fair ainsi que du magazine et laboratoire artistique et critique AFRIKADAA. En discussion avec Marly Jean-Noel, organisatrice en 2026 de l’exposition et conférence L’expérience noire en design et Victoria Owusu, designer créative spécialisée en identité visuelle et stratégie de contenu.

entry.title: Voices of Quebec | Les Voix du Québec

media:group.media:title: Voices of Quebec | Les Voix du Québec
media:group.media:description:
Join us for this student-led roundtable that offers an introduction to the linguistic landscape of Quebec and brings four language experts, each speaking to the space occupied by the four major language groups in Quebec, namely the French language, the English language, Indigenous languages (including revitalization) and finally, Heritage languages (spoken among immigrants in Quebec).
Rejoignez-nous pour cette table ronde animée par des étudiants qui propose une introduction au paysage linguistique du Québec et réunisse quatre experts en langues, qui s’expriment chacun sur la place occupée par les quatre principaux groupes linguistiques au Québec, à savoir la langue française, la langue anglaise, les langues autochtones (y compris leur revitalisation) et enfin, les langues d’origine (parlées par les immigrant·e·s au Québec).
Organized by: Isha Jain; Romain Chambon; Patrick Lewis With: Université de Montréal, Anthropology department

entry.title: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation: Confronting Our Past

media:group.media:title: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation: Confronting Our Past
media:group.media:description:
Join us as the Office of Indigenous Directions invites the university community to participate in a day of reflection and learning, following the publication of a long-awaited report, Exploring Concordia’s Colonial Past.
A panel discussion about the report on Concordia's colonial past and its contents is moderated by Peter Gossage (Distinguished Professor Emeritus, Dept. of History), with the participation of: • Colby Gaudet, the report's author and SSHRC Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of History at Dalhousie University • Kahérakwas Donna Goodleaf, Director, Decolonizing Curriculum and Pedagogy • Sigwan Thivierge, Associate Professor, First Peoples Studies & Linguistics • Lisa White, Executive Director, Equity Office
00:02 4th Space Intro 01:26 Opening remakrds Manon Tremblay 06:11 Panel Introduction 07:39 Exploring Concordia's Colonial Past, Presentation by Colby Gaudet 37:35 Panel Discussion 01:19:12 Q&A 01:57:36 Final Thoughts
About the report:
In 2021, Concordia commissioned then doctoral student Colby Gaudet to investigate the university’s historical foundations and produce a report that would help situate the university’s past within the wider context of colonialism and Indigenous experiences.
The research focused on the Grey Nuns, whose former motherhouse is part of Concordia’s campus, the founding institutions of Loyola College and Sir George Williams University and their respective connections to the Jesuits and the YMCA, all of which played roles in broader colonial systems in Canada.
By examining these histories, the report invites the Concordia community to reflect on the university’s past and to support ongoing efforts toward reconciliation and decolonization.
You can download the report here: https://www.concordia.ca/indigenous/resources/colonial-past.html

entry.title: Fair Trade at Concordia with Shatha Arslan and Sofia Melatti

media:group.media:title: Fair Trade at Concordia with Shatha Arslan and Sofia Melatti
media:group.media:description: Concordia University is a Fair Trade certified campus; offering a range of Fairtrade product availability for students and faculty while hosting events for engagement. Fairtrade is an ethical certification and sustainability label that puts farmers’ rights at the forefront, ensuring they get paid a fair livable wage. Join us as we present the necessary steps towards gold status campus designation, our outreach with the Concordia community, and our engagement with the academic faculty.
